title: The (으) Rule: Consonant vs Vowel Stems
plainEnglish: Dozens of endings add an extra 으 (or use 을/ㄹ) only when the stem ends in a consonant (받침).
whenToUse: Apply it every time you attach an ending written with (으): -(으)면, -(으)세요, -(으)ㄹ 수 있다, -(으)ㄴ/ㄹ, -(으)니까, -(으)러, -(으)려고, -(으)ㄹ게요.
attachmentRule: Look at the stem's last syllable. HAS a 받침 (consonant ending) → use the 으 form: 먹다 → 먹을 수 있다, 먹으면, 먹으세요, 먹은. NO 받침 (vowel ending) → drop the 으: 가다 → 갈 수 있다, 가면, 가세요, 간. The 으 is just a helper so two consonants don't crash together. Exception: ㄹ-stems (살다) drop their ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ endings (사세요, 사니까, 삽니다).
contrastWith: This is exactly the 갈 수 있다 (vowel stem 가-) vs 먹을 수 있다 (consonant stem 먹-) difference. Same ending, but 먹- needs the 으/을 helper and 가- does not.

examples.en: come → can come (vowel stem, no 으)
receive → can receive (consonant stem, +을)
see → if (you) see (vowel stem)
sit → if (you) sit (consonant stem, +으)

commonMistakes: Adding 으 to a vowel stem: 가으면 is wrong → 가면.
Dropping 으 from a consonant stem: 먹면 is wrong → 먹으면.
Forgetting ㄹ-stems are special: 살다 → 사세요 (the ㄹ disappears).
studyOrder: Find the stem (drop 다)
Check: does it end in a 받침?
Yes → add 으/을; No → skip the 으
Remember ㄹ-stem exceptions
beginnerExplanation: This one rule answers your 갈 수 vs 먹을 수 question — and it controls dozens of endings. When an ending is written with (으) in parentheses, you only use that 으 if the verb stem ends in a consonant (a 받침). 먹- ends in ㄱ, so you say 먹을 수 있어요 and 먹으면. 가- ends in a vowel, so you just say 갈 수 있어요 and 가면. Think of 으 as a tiny cushion that keeps two consonants from colliding. Master this and half of Korean conjugation suddenly makes sense.

title: Liaison: Linking 받침 to the Next Vowel
plainEnglish: A final consonant (받침) slides over to start the next syllable when that syllable begins with a vowel.
whenToUse: It happens automatically in pronunciation whenever a 받침 is followed by a syllable that starts with ㅇ (a vowel sound).
attachmentRule: 받침 + ㅇ-vowel → the 받침 becomes the next syllable's first sound. 꽃이 sounds like 꼬치, 한국어 like 한구거, 음악 like 으막, 옷을 like 오슬. With a double 받침, only the SECOND consonant moves over: 읽어 sounds like 일거.
contrastWith: The spelling never changes — only the sound links. This is why 읽어요 (written) is pronounced 일거요. Learners who read block-by-block sound robotic; linking makes you sound natural.

examples.en: Korean language — sounds like 한구거
The flower is pretty — 꽃이 sounds like 꼬치
I read a book — sounds like 채글 일거요
I go home — 집에 sounds like 지베

commonMistakes: Pronouncing each block separately (꽃#이) instead of linking to 꼬치.
Moving the wrong consonant in a double 받침 — only the second one links.
studyOrder: Spot a 받침 followed by a ㅇ-vowel syllable
Slide the 받침 into that syllable
For double 받침, move only the second one
Read whole words, not block-by-block
beginnerExplanation: Korean words flow together. When a syllable ends in a consonant and the next one starts with a vowel (the silent ㅇ), that consonant hops over and is pronounced at the start of the next syllable. So 한국어 is written in three blocks but sounds like 한구거, and 꽃이 sounds like 꼬치. The spelling stays put; only your mouth links them. This single habit is the biggest step from sounding like a textbook to sounding like a person.

title: Nasalization
plainEnglish: The stop sounds ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ turn into the nasal sounds ㅇ/ㄴ/ㅁ when followed by ㄴ or ㅁ.
whenToUse: It happens automatically when a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ-type 받침 meets a following ㄴ or ㅁ — extremely common in -습니다/-ㅂ니다 verbs.
attachmentRule: Before ㄴ or ㅁ: ㄱ(ㅋ,ㄲ) → ㅇ(ng); ㄷ(ㅅ,ㅆ,ㅈ,ㅊ,ㅌ) → ㄴ; ㅂ(ㅍ) → ㅁ. So 학년 → 항년, 입니다 → 임니다, 닫는 → 단는, 먹는 → 멍는, 끝나다 → 끈나다.
contrastWith: Like liaison, it is a SOUND change only; spelling is unchanged. It's why polite 합니다 sounds like 함니다.

examples.en: Thank you — sounds like 감사함니다
Korean (language) — sounds like 한궁말
It ends — sounds like 끈나요
a person who eats — 먹는 sounds like 멍는

commonMistakes: Saying 학년 literally instead of 항년.
studyOrder: Spot a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ 받침 before ㄴ or ㅁ
ㄱ→ㅇ, ㄷ→ㄴ, ㅂ→ㅁ
Apply it to every -습니다/-ㅂ니다
Trust your ears over the spelling
beginnerExplanation: When a 'hard stop' consonant (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ) bumps into a nasal sound (ㄴ or ㅁ), it 'goes nasal' to match: ㄱ→ㅇ, ㄷ→ㄴ, ㅂ→ㅁ. The most useful place to notice this is the polite ending: 합니다 is pronounced 함니다, and 입니다 is 임니다. It's the same reason 학년 (school year) sounds like 항년. You don't change the spelling — your mouth just smooths the two sounds together.

title: Palatalization
plainEnglish: A 받침 ㄷ or ㅌ becomes a ㅈ/ㅊ sound when the next syllable is 이 (or 히).
whenToUse: It happens when ㄷ/ㅌ at the end of a stem meets 이 or 히 — common in 같이, 굳이, 붙이다, and 닫히다.
attachmentRule: ㄷ + 이 → 지 (ji): 굳이 → 구지, 해돋이 → 해도지. ㅌ + 이 → 치 (chi): 같이 → 가치, 붙이다 → 부치다. ㄷ + 히 → 치: 닫히다 → 다치다. It only triggers before 이/히 — not before other vowels.
contrastWith: Only before 이/히. 같이 is 가치, but 같아 is just 가타 (no change). This is why romanizing 같이 as 'gati' is wrong — it's gachi.

examples.en: Let's go together — 같이 sounds like 가치
You don't have to bother — 굳이 sounds like 구지
to stick a sticker — 붙이다 sounds like 부치다
the door closes — 닫히다 sounds like 다치다

commonMistakes: Saying 가티 for 같이 — it's 가치.
Applying it before other vowels: 같아 stays 가타, not 가차.
studyOrder: Spot a ㄷ/ㅌ 받침 right before 이 or 히
ㄷ→ㅈ(지), ㅌ→ㅊ(치)
Only before 이/히, no other vowel
Apply to 같이, 굳이, 붙이다…
beginnerExplanation: When a ㄷ or ㅌ at the end of a syllable runs into the vowel 이, your tongue is already near the roof of your mouth, so the sound shifts to ㅈ/ㅊ. That's why the very common word 같이 ('together') is pronounced 가치, not 'ga-ti.' Likewise 굳이 sounds like 구지. It only happens before 이 (or 히) — 같아 is still 가타. Once you know this, those 'why does it sound like that?' moments disappear.

title: Aspiration
plainEnglish: ㅎ merges with a neighboring ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ to form the breathy ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ.
whenToUse: When a 받침 ㅎ meets ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅈ, or when a 받침 ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ meets ㅎ — common in 좋다, 축하, 못하다, 입학.
attachmentRule: 받침 ㅎ + ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅈ → ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅊ: 좋다 → 조타, 놓고 → 노코, 많지 → 만치. 받침 ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ + ㅎ → aspirated: 축하 → 추카, 입학 → 이팍, 못하다 → 모타다, 백화점 → 배콰점.
contrastWith: It's a merge, not a drop — the ㅎ doesn't vanish silently, it 'aspirates' the other consonant. So 좋다 is 조타 (with a strong t), not 조다.

examples.en: to be good — sounds like 조타
Congratulations — sounds like 추카해요
entrance exam — 입학 sounds like 이팍
I can't do it — 못해요 sounds like 모태요

commonMistakes: Saying 조다 for 좋다 — it's 조타.
Saying 축하 block-by-block instead of 추카.
studyOrder: Spot ㅎ next to ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ (either order)
They merge into ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ
Apply to 좋다, 축하, 못하다
Listen for the puff of air
beginnerExplanation: The letter ㅎ is friendly — it merges with a neighbor instead of staying separate. When ㅎ touches ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ (in either order), the pair becomes one breathy consonant: ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ. So 좋다 is 조타, 축하 is 추카, and 못해요 is 모태요. The air 'puffs' out. This is why congratulations (축하) never sounds like 'chuk-ha' — it's 추카.

title: Tensification
plainEnglish: Plain consonants ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅅ/ㅈ become the tense ㄲ/ㄸ/ㅃ/ㅆ/ㅉ right after a stop 받침.
whenToUse: After a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ-type 받침, a following plain consonant tightens — very common in everyday words like 학교, 식당, 숙제.
attachmentRule: 받침 ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ (and family) + ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅅ/ㅈ → tense: 학교 → 학꾜, 먹다 → 먹따, 식당 → 식땅, 숙제 → 숙쩨, 입국 → 입꾹. It also appears after some ㄴ/ㄹ endings (갈게요 → 갈께요).
contrastWith: Spelling shows the plain consonant, but you pronounce the tense one. 학교 is written with ㄱ but said with ㄲ (학꾜).

examples.en: I go to school — 학교 sounds like 학꾜
I eat at a restaurant — 식당 sounds like 식땅
Did you do the homework? — 숙제 sounds like 숙쩨
I'll go — 갈게요 sounds like 갈께요

commonMistakes: Saying a soft 학교 instead of the tense 학꾜.
Expecting the spelling to show ㄲ/ㄸ — it doesn't; only the sound is tense.
studyOrder: Spot a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ 받침 before a plain consonant
Tighten it: ㄱ→ㄲ, ㄷ→ㄸ, ㅂ→ㅃ, ㅅ→ㅆ, ㅈ→ㅉ
Apply to 학교, 식당, 숙제
Trust the sound, not the spelling
beginnerExplanation: After a hard stop (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ at the end of a syllable), the next plain consonant gets 'squeezed' into a tense one. So 학교 sounds like 학꾜, 식당 like 식땅, and 숙제 like 숙쩨. The spelling still shows the soft consonant, but native speakers say the tense version automatically. You'll do it naturally once your ear gets used to it — for now, just know that 'school' is 학꾜, not a gentle 'hak-gyo.'

title: Irregular Verb Types
plainEnglish: Seven groups of verbs/adjectives whose stem changes before certain endings instead of staying fixed.
whenToUse: Recognize the type from the stem's last letter, then apply its change when adding vowel endings like -아/어요 or -(으) endings.
attachmentRule: ㅂ-irregular: 덥다 → 더워요, 돕다 → 도와요. ㄷ-irregular: 듣다 → 들어요, 걷다 → 걸어요. ㅅ-irregular: 짓다 → 지어요, 낫다 → 나아요. 르-irregular: 빠르다 → 빨라요, 모르다 → 몰라요. ㅡ-drop: 쓰다 → 써요, 바쁘다 → 바빠요. ㄹ-irregular: 살다 → 살아요 but 사세요/삽니다 (ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ). ㅎ-irregular (adjectives): 빨갛다 → 빨개요, 어떻다 → 어때요.
contrastWith: Regular verbs keep the stem (먹다 → 먹어요). Irregulars change it (듣다 → 들어요, not 듣어요). The trigger is usually a vowel ending; before consonant endings many stay regular.

examples.en: The weather is so hot. (ㅂ: 덥다→더워요)
I listen to music. (ㄷ: 듣다→들어요)
He's fast. (르: 빠르다→빨라요)
I write a letter. (ㅡ: 쓰다→써요)

commonMistakes: Treating an irregular like a regular: 듣어요 → it's 들어요.
Over-applying: not every ㅂ/ㄷ/ㅅ verb is irregular (받다 → 받아요 is regular).
Forgetting ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ (살다 → 삽니다).
studyOrder: Identify the stem's last letter
Match it to one of the 7 irregular types
Apply the change before vowel endings
Memorize which common verbs are exceptions
beginnerExplanation: Most Korean verbs are predictable, but seven small groups bend their stem before certain endings. For example, ㄷ-verbs like 듣다 (to hear) turn the ㄷ into ㄹ before a vowel: 들어요, not 듣어요. ㅂ-verbs like 덥다 (hot) become 더워요. 르-verbs like 빠르다 (fast) become 빨라요. Don't try to memorize all at once — learn the type when you meet a common verb, and soon you'll feel the pattern. Watch out: not every verb that ends in ㅂ/ㄷ/ㅅ is irregular (받다 is regular: 받아요).
